questions.question: What is the two-pointer technique and when do you use it?
questions.title: Two Pointer Technique Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Two pointers** use two indices — typically one at each end or both starting from the same point — moving toward or away from each other based on conditions. It turns many O(n²) problems into O(n) by avoiding nested loops on sorted or structured data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Pattern recognition — knowing when a problem structure allows two pointers instead of brute force
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not recognizing that two pointers often require sorted input, or confusing it with the fast/slow pointer variant
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name 3-4 concrete problems that use two pointers and explain the invariant each maintains

sections.title: Two Pointers: Moving Toward Each Other
sections.content: **Classic form (opposite ends)**: `left = 0`, `right = n-1`. Move inward based on a condition. Example: pair sum in sorted array — if `arr[left] + arr[right] == target`, found; if too small, `left++`; if too large, `right--`. Works because the sorted order guarantees that moving left inward increases the sum and moving right inward decreases it. **Same direction form**: both start at 0, one leads (fast), one trails (slow) — used for removing duplicates, sliding window variants.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Opposite ends: pair sum, palindrome check, container with most water
- Same direction (fast/slow): remove duplicates in-place, cycle detection
- Usually requires sorted array for the opposite-ends variant
- Eliminates nested loop: O(n²) → O(n)
- Each pointer moves at most n steps total — O(n)
- Palindrome: compare arr[left] == arr[right], move inward
- Three-sum: fix one element, two-pointer on the rest

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The two-pointer technique places one pointer at each end of a sorted array and moves them inward based on a condition. For the pair sum problem on a sorted array, if the sum of the two elements is too small I move the left pointer right to increase it, and if too large I move the right pointer left to decrease it. This avoids checking every pair — O(n) instead of O(n squared). I'd mention that the sorted precondition is usually required for the opposite-ends variant, and that the same concept extends to three-sum by fixing one element and applying two pointers to the rest.

questions.question: How do you check if a string is a palindrome using two pointers?
questions.title: Palindrome Check Two Pointers Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use two pointers — one at each end — moving inward.** If characters at both pointers match, move inward. If they don't match, it's not a palindrome. If the pointers cross without a mismatch, it is a palindrome. O(n) time, O(1) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Simple two-pointer application — used to verify you know the basic technique before harder variants
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reversing the string and comparing (valid but O(n) space) without knowing the O(1) space two-pointer approach
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Offer both approaches, then show the O(1) space two-pointer as the preferred solution and handle the edge case of ignoring non-alphanumeric characters

sections.title: Meet in the Middle
sections.content: Initialize `left = 0`, `right = s.length() - 1`. While `left < right`: if `s.charAt(left) != s.charAt(right)` — return false. Else: `left++`, `right--`. After loop — return true. **Common variant** (valid palindrome ignoring non-alphanumeric): inside the loop, skip non-alphanumeric with `while (left < right && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(left))) left++` — similarly for right.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Two pointer: O(n) time, O(1) space
- Reverse and compare: O(n) time, O(n) space
- Left < right condition (not <=, single char is palindrome)
- Common variant: ignore spaces and punctuation
- Character.isLetterOrDigit() and Character.toLowerCase() for normalization
- Works for any sequence: arrays, strings, linked lists (with extra steps)
- Even-length: pointers never equal; odd-length: they meet at middle

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use two pointers, one at each end of the string. While left is less than right, I compare the characters at both pointers. If they don't match, it's not a palindrome and I return false. If they match, I move both pointers inward. If the loop completes without a mismatch, it's a palindrome. This is O(n) time and O(1) space, which is better than reversing the string which costs O(n) space. For the variant that ignores non-alphanumeric characters, I skip them with a while loop before each comparison.

questions.question: How do you remove duplicates from a sorted array in-place?
questions.title: Remove Duplicates Sorted Array Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use a slow pointer tracking the position of the last unique element, and a fast pointer scanning ahead.** When `arr[fast] != arr[slow]`, copy `arr[fast]` to `arr[slow+1]` and increment slow. Return `slow + 1` as the new length. O(n) time, O(1) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: In-place array manipulation with two pointers — a fundamental skill
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a new array or ArrayList to collect unique elements instead of modifying in-place
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify that the problem modifies the array in-place and returns the new logical length — elements beyond that length don't matter

sections.title: Slow-Fast Pointer: In-Place Compaction
sections.content: For sorted arrays, duplicates are adjacent. Use `slow = 0` (position of last unique written) and `fast` iterating from 1. If `arr[fast] == arr[slow]` — duplicate, skip (fast++). If `arr[fast] != arr[slow]` — new unique element: `slow++`, then `arr[slow] = arr[fast]`. After the loop, the unique elements occupy `arr[0..slow]` and the new length is `slow + 1`. Elements beyond the new length are irrelevant.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Works only because array is sorted (duplicates are adjacent)
- slow: tracks last written unique position
- fast: scans ahead looking for new unique values
- When arr[fast] != arr[slow]: write to arr[slow+1] and advance slow
- Return slow + 1 (count, not index)
- Time: O(n), Space: O(1) in-place
- Variant: allow at most 2 duplicates — change condition to arr[fast] != arr[slow-1]

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Since the array is sorted, all duplicates are adjacent. I use two pointers: slow starting at 0 and fast at 1. Fast scans forward. When it finds an element different from arr[slow], that's a new unique value — I increment slow and copy the element there. When they're the same, I just advance fast. At the end, unique elements are in positions 0 through slow, and I return slow plus one as the new length. This modifies the array in place using O(1) space. I'd also mention the variant where you allow at most two occurrences by comparing to the element two positions back.

questions.question: How do you solve the three-sum problem using two pointers?
questions.title: Three Sum Java Two Pointers | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Sort the array, fix one element with an outer loop, then apply two pointers on the remaining sorted subarray.** For each fixed element, find pairs in the rest that sum to `target - fixed`. Skip duplicates to avoid duplicate triplets. O(n²) time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can combine sorting + two pointers, and handle the duplicate-skipping edge case
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not skipping duplicates after finding a triplet, resulting in duplicate results, or trying to use HashMap instead of sorting first
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clearly explain the duplicate-skipping logic at both the outer loop and inner pointer levels

sections.title: Sort + Fix + Two Pointers
sections.content: Sort the array first — O(n log n). Outer loop: fix element at index `i`. If `i > 0 && arr[i] == arr[i-1]`, skip (duplicate outer element). Inner: `left = i+1`, `right = n-1`. While `left < right`: compute `sum = arr[i] + arr[left] + arr[right]`. If sum == 0: add triplet, skip duplicates (`while left < right && arr[left] == arr[left+1] left++`), then move both pointers. If sum < 0: `left++`. If sum > 0: `right--`. Total: **O(n²)**.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Sort first: O(n log n)
- Outer loop fixes one element — O(n)
- Inner two pointers on rest — O(n) per outer iteration
- Total: O(n²)
- Skip duplicates at outer loop: arr[i] == arr[i-1]
- Skip duplicates at inner pointers after finding a triplet
- Early termination: if arr[i] > 0, all remaining sums are positive — break
- Space: O(1) for the algorithm itself (sort may use O(log n) stack)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Three-sum extends two-sum by fixing one element at a time with an outer loop, then applying two pointers to the remaining sorted subarray. I sort first — O(n log n). For each index i, if the current element is the same as the previous one I skip it to avoid duplicate triplets. Then with left at i plus 1 and right at the last index, I apply the standard two-pointer approach looking for pairs that sum to negative arr[i]. When I find a match, I advance both pointers and skip any duplicates. Total time complexity is O(n squared) because for each of the n outer iterations I do O(n) inner work.

questions.question: How do you use two pointers to find a pair with a given sum in a sorted array?
questions.title: Two Pointers: Pair with Given Sum in Sorted Array
questions.direct_answer: Place left at index 0 and right at n-1; move left right when the sum is too small, move right left when too large, and return the pair when equal — O(n) vs O(n²) brute force.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can exploit sorted-order to eliminate candidates directionally
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using nested loops for O(n²) instead of recognising the two-pointer opportunity
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why sorted order lets you make a confident directional decision at every step

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Start by explaining the setup. I place two pointers — left at index 0, right at the last index. I then compute the sum of the two elements. If the sum equals the target, I've found my pair and return it. If the sum is less than the target, I move the left pointer right to get a larger value — because the array is sorted, every element to the right of left is strictly bigger. If the sum is greater, I move the right pointer left to get a smaller value. I keep doing this until the pointers cross.

The key insight is that sorted order gives us decision power. At each step we know with certainty whether to increase or decrease the sum, so we never need to revisit any element. That gives us O(n) time and O(1) space, compared to the brute-force O(n²) approach of checking every pair.

I always mention the edge cases: what if no pair exists (pointers cross without a match), what about duplicate values, and what if the array has fewer than two elements. Interviewers appreciate seeing you think about boundary conditions without being prompted.

sections.title: Key Points
content: left = 0, right = n-1; move left++ when sum < target, right-- when sum > target
Works only on sorted arrays — sorted order enables directional decisions
O(n) time, O(1) space vs O(n²) brute force
Handle edge cases: no pair found, fewer than 2 elements, duplicates

questions.question: Explain the 'slow and fast pointer' technique with a concrete example.
questions.title: Slow and Fast Pointer (Floyd's Algorithm) Explained
questions.direct_answer: The slow pointer moves one step at a time while the fast pointer moves two; if they ever meet inside a linked list, a cycle exists — this is Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm.

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with pointer-based linked-list algorithms beyond basic traversal
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning cycle detection and forgetting the 'find middle' use-case
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why the two pointers must meet inside the cycle (the mathematical reason) and name all three classic applications

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The slow-and-fast pointer pattern, also called Floyd's algorithm, uses two pointers that traverse a data structure at different speeds — slow moves one node at a time and fast moves two nodes at a time.

The most common use is cycle detection in a linked list. If a cycle exists, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow pointer and they meet inside the cycle. If there is no cycle, the fast pointer reaches null first. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, far better than storing visited nodes in a HashSet.

A second use is finding the middle of a linked list. When the fast pointer reaches the end (null or the last node), the slow pointer is exactly at the midpoint. This is useful when you need to split a list, for example in merge sort on linked lists.

A third, more advanced use is finding the start of a cycle: after the two pointers meet, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time — the point where they meet again is the cycle's entry node.

I always clarify upfront which problem I am solving, because each application uses the same technique but a slightly different exit condition.

sections.title: Key Points
content: slow moves +1, fast moves +2; if they meet → cycle exists
When fast reaches end (no meeting) → no cycle
Finding middle: when fast is at end, slow is at mid
Finding cycle start: after meeting, reset one pointer to head, advance both by 1 until they meet again
O(n) time, O(1) space — no HashSet needed
